transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi Dr. Smith. Well, um, it's actually been a really frustrating time lately, and I guess I came in because things are getting incredibly complicated with my work. I’m an artist, and usually, I’m very good at communicating my vision—I mean, I have my degree, I know how to talk to galleries and clients, I know how to pitch a concept. But recently, my artist statements, the emails and notes I send to clients, and honestly even just what I say out loud when we're sitting in planning meetings... it's all just falling apart. 

People just keep stopping me and telling me they absolutely cannot follow what I’m trying to explain. And it’s so frustrating because to me, the connections are completely obvious and necessary to the art. Like, I’ll be talking about the physical textures of a canvas, you know, how the layering of the impasto works, and then naturally that makes me think about the financial constraints of the materials, so I'll jump to the budgets, and then from the budgets, it just makes perfect sense to talk about the secret meanings behind the resource allocation and the hidden messages I'm weaving into the piece itself. But apparently, jumping from textures to budgets to secret meanings just confuses everyone. They just sit there blinking at me, and it’s starting to really affect my commissions because they think I'm not making any sense at all, even though I'm just trying to give them the full, complete picture of what I'm creating.

During these periods where your speech feels hard for others to follow, have you noticed feeling unusually energetic, needing much less sleep than normal, or feeling like your thoughts are racing faster than you can keep up with?

Oh, the energy, yes, absolutely. It's actually been incredible, honestly, because usually, I'm someone who absolutely needs a solid eight hours of sleep, you know? Like, if I don't get my full rest, I'm usually just dragging all day, I can't even look at a canvas, the colors just look completely muddy and flat to me, and I can't focus. 

But lately... lately it's like someone just flipped a master switch in my brain. I'll be in the studio, and the ideas are just coming so fast, just layering and layering, and I'll be working so late, mixing oils, trying to get the exact right texture for the impasto I was telling you about, and suddenly I look at the clock and it's 4 AM. And the crazy part is, I'll go lay down for maybe two or three hours tops, and then my eyes just snap open. And I'm not groggy at all! I wake up feeling completely bright and totally ready to keep going. 

I just jump right out of bed and go straight back to the easel. I'm not tired the way I normally would be after a night like that. It's like my body doesn't even need the rest right now because the work is just demanding to be let out, and my thoughts are just moving so quickly to keep up with all the inspiration. I could just keep painting and painting, and it feels amazing, honestly, to have that kind of drive, even if other people are getting confused by how fast I'm moving through the concepts.

Have there been any periods in your life where you felt this same confusion in your speech or had trouble communicating your thoughts clearly even when you were feeling completely normal and not experiencing this extra energy?

Well, um, it wasn't exactly that my speech was racing like it is now, but it was definitely still hard to communicate clearly with people, mostly because of everything else that was going on. 

It's actually really interesting you bring that up, because there was this period—maybe for about a month or so, earlier this year, right around the time I was trying to organize my inventory—where things were actually very quiet for me physically. I mean, my energy was completely baseline. I wasn't feeling unstoppable or driven like I do right now. I was actually sleeping my normal eight hours, getting up, making my morning coffee, and going into the studio at a completely average time. I wasn't staying up until 4 AM at all. 

But even though my body and my energy felt totally normal, my mind was... well, things were still incredibly intense and confusing for several weeks. Because during that quieter month, I kept hearing these comments coming from right behind the heavy wooden storage shelves in my studio. It was like people were standing just out of sight, murmuring and whispering about me, critiquing what I was doing. I would stop and look, and of course, no one was physically back there, but the comments just kept happening. 

And on top of that, I started reading these intense, hidden warnings into completely ordinary studio materials. I would look at a standard tube of cadmium red paint, or the way the turpentine was separating in its glass jar, and I would just instantly realize that there was a very specific, deliberate warning coded into it. Like the universe or the materials themselves were telling me that something terrible would happen if I used that specific brush or mixed those certain pigments. It was exhausting. So, even though I was sleeping normally and didn't have that crazy extra energy, I was still so distracted by the voices behind the shelves and all those hidden warnings for weeks that I couldn't really explain to anyone why I was acting so strangely or why I refused to use half the supplies in my own studio.
During that month when you were hearing those voices and noticing the warnings, did you feel like your mood was entirely normal, or were you feeling notably depressed or down?

Well, no, not at all, actually. It’s funny you ask that, because I think a lot of people assume that if you're struggling to get your work done or if you're avoiding certain things—like me avoiding half my art supplies—that you must be depressed. But I wasn't feeling down in the slightest. My mood was completely, perfectly normal. 

I mean, I wasn't sad, I wasn't crying, I didn't have that heavy, empty feeling you hear people talk about when they're depressed. Emotionally, I was totally fine. Like I was saying before, I was still getting up at my regular time, and I still had my whole morning routine. I do this very specific pour-over coffee every morning, it takes exactly eight minutes to get the bloom just right, and I was still doing that every single day, enjoying the smell of the beans, looking out the window at the morning light. I feel like if I were depressed, I wouldn't have cared about the light or the coffee, right? But I still cared about all of that. 

I felt completely baseline in my heart, I guess you could say. It was purely just... logistical exhaustion, if that makes sense? Because I was actually perfectly content and just wanted to get my canvases prepped, but I was constantly having to navigate around the whispering from the shelves, and having to spend all this mental energy second-guessing if the cadmium red or the turpentine was safe to use that day. So my mood itself was totally fine, just... occupied. Really, really busy trying to decode everything and stay safe from the warnings. But not sad. Not down at all. Honestly, I remember feeling almost entirely neutral emotionally, just highly focused on what the materials were trying to tell me.

Outside of those periods when you were hearing voices or feeling that burst of energy, have you ever experienced these same difficulties with your speech and communication during times when you felt completely stable and clear-headed?

No, not really. I mean, when everything is just... normal, when I'm not having those surges where I'm painting until the sun comes up, and I'm not dealing with the, you know, the whispering or the warnings from the turpentine, my speech is totally fine. I don't stumble over my words or jump around so much that people can't follow me. 

Like, when I'm just having a regular Tuesday, going to the art supply store—there's this great little independent shop downtown, they always have the best selection of natural bristle brushes, the kind that don't shed into your gesso—when I go there and talk to the owner, or when I'm just chatting with my friends over lunch, I can explain exactly what I'm thinking without any problem. I don't get that feeling where my mouth just can't keep up with my brain, or where I'm losing the thread of what I was trying to say halfway through a sentence. 

It's really only when things get so heightened with the energy, or when my brain is so preoccupied with all those hidden messages, that my communication gets messy. When I'm clear-headed, I'm very articulate. I actually pride myself on being able to explain my artistic process really clearly to people who don't paint, which takes a lot of careful communication, you know? Because you have to translate visual concepts into words, and if my speech was always disorganized, I'd never be able to do that. So yeah, when I'm stable, I'm completely coherent. It's just those other times that get complicated.

Looking back over the last year or so, what is the total amount of time you have spent experiencing those voices and hidden messages, versus the time you've spent in those high-energy, sleep-deprived periods?

Well, um, if I really sit down and think about the whole year in its entirety—which is kind of hard to do, honestly, because time feels so fluid when you're working on a big series of paintings, you know? Like, January bleeds into February, and suddenly it's summer and you're still working on the same themes. But if I try to map it out, I would definitely say that the high-energy periods, those stretches where I’m just completely wired, irritable, and painting non-stop without needing to sleep... those have definitely taken up the majority of the year. 

I mean, even though the intensity of that energy kind of ebbs and flows—like, sometimes I'm just staying up until 2 AM, and other times I literally don't close my eyes for three days straight because I'm so driven—that overall state of being revved up and overproductive has definitely been the dominant theme of my year. It's like this constant hum in the background that just keeps pushing me forward, even when it gets exhausting. 

The quieter time, that month or so I told you about where my energy was totally baseline but I was dealing with the voices behind the shelves and all the warnings in the turpentine... that was definitely a distinct period, but it was much shorter in comparison. It was just that one specific stretch where my body felt calm but my mind was so overwhelmed by the messages. But yeah, if you look at the whole year, the vast majority of it has been spent in that energized, irritable, can't-stop-working kind of state. The calmer stretches, even with the voices, were definitely the exception rather than the rule.
